content: 1. A study conducted by Morley in 1999 evaluated the Bayley Mental Development Index (MDI) and Psychomotor Development Index (PDI) in children aged 12-23 months. The study compared the effects of animal milk versus follow-on formula when administered at 9 months of age. The evidence was of low certainty. 2. No data was available regarding the prevalence of anemia in children consuming animal milk versus follow-on formula. 3. Two studies (Akkermans 2016 and Lovell 2018) reported on iron deficiency anemia (IDA) in children aged 12-23 months. These studies provided moderate certainty evidence, showing that follow-on formula may reduce the risk of IDA compared to animal milk. 4. Two studies (Akkermans 2016 and Lovell 2018) also assessed iron deficiency (defined as serum ferritin <12 g/L) in children aged 12-23 months. Moderate certainty evidence suggested that follow-on formula likely increases ferritin concentrations compared to animal milk. 5. Five studies (Akkermans 2016, Daly 1996, Lovell 2018, Maldonado 2007, and Morley 1999) examined hemoglobin concentrations in children aged 12-23 months. Moderate certainty evidence indicated that follow-on formula may improve hemoglobin levels compared to animal milk. 6. Subgroup analyses revealed that follow-on formula likely increases ferritin concentrations in children aged 12-23 months, regardless of whether the study was funded by private industry or not. 7. A single study (Akkermans 2016) reported on stool frequency and consistency in children aged 12-23 months. The study found that follow-on formula may make little or no difference in stool consistency compared to animal milk. 8. No data was available on outcomes such as nutrient intakes, feeding practices, oral health, morbidity, dietary diversity, gut health, or allergy prevalence in children consuming animal milk versus follow-on formula. 9. One study (Svahn 1999) compared full-fat animal milk to lower-fat milk in children aged 12-23 months. The study was assessed as having a low risk of bias for confounding, attrition, and performance bias but a high risk of detection bias. 10. No data was available on critical outcomes such as growth, body composition, long-term food preferences, or dietary patterns in children consuming full-fat versus lower-fat milk. 11. One study (Svahn 1999) reported on serum lipid profiles in children aged 12-23 months. Low certainty evidence suggested that lower-fat milk may make little or no difference in serum cholesterol, LDL, HDL, or triglycerides compared to full-fat milk. 12. A single study (Svahn 1999) compared animal milk to plant-based milk in children aged 12-23 months. Low certainty evidence indicated that plant-based milk may make little or no difference in serum cholesterol, LDL, HDL, or triglycerides compared to animal milk. 13. Eight studies (Rivera 2010, Sazawal 2007, Stecksén-Blicks 2009, Stekel 1986, Stekel 1988, Svahn 1999, Szymlek-Gay 2009, and Villalpando 2006) compared animal milk to fortified milk in children aged 12-23 months. These studies provided data for the synthesis of this review. 14. One study (Svahn 1999) reported on weight outcomes in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Low certainty evidence suggested no significant differences in weight between the groups. 15. One study (Sazawal 2007) reported on stunting and wasting in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Low certainty evidence suggested that fortified milk may reduce the prevalence of stunting and wasting compared to animal milk. 16. Two studies (Stekel 1988 and Svahn 1999) reported on serum iron concentrations in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Low certainty evidence suggested that fortified milk may improve serum iron levels compared to animal milk. 17. Two studies (Sazawal 2007 and Villalpando 2006) reported on plasma zinc concentrations in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Low certainty evidence suggested that fortified milk may improve plasma zinc levels compared to animal milk. 18. Three studies (Rivera 2010, Sazawal 2007, and Stekel 1986) reported on anemia outcomes in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Low certainty evidence suggested that fortified milk may reduce the prevalence of anemia compared to animal milk. 19. Six studies (Sazawal 2007, Stekel 1986, Stekel 1988, Svahn 1999, Szymlek-Gay 2009, and Villalpando 2006) reported on hemoglobin concentrations in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Moderate certainty evidence suggested that fortified milk likely improves hemoglobin levels compared to animal milk. 20. Three studies (Sazawal 2007, Stekel 1988, and Szymlek-Gay 2009) reported on ferritin concentrations in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Moderate certainty evidence suggested that fortified milk likely increases ferritin levels compared to animal milk. 21. One study (Stecksén-Blicks 2009) reported on oral health outcomes in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Low certainty evidence suggested no significant differences in the mean decayed, missing, and filled surfaces (dmfs) index between the groups. 22. One study (Stekel 1988) reported on respiratory and diarrhea episodes in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. Low certainty evidence suggested no significant differences in morbidity outcomes between the groups. 23. No data was available on outcomes such as dietary diversity, gut health, allergy prevalence, or phytoestrogen-related outcomes in children consuming animal milk versus fortified milk. 24. A cross-sectional study (Ghisolfi 2012) reported that daily consumption of 250 mL of cow’s milk in children aged 12-23 months increased the risk of insufficient intakes of several nutrients, including linoleic acid, alpha-linolenic acid, iron, vitamin C, and vitamin D. These deficiencies were less prevalent in children consuming follow-on formula. 25. Another study (Gill 1997) compared follow-on formula with added iron to regular formula and animal milk. The study found that hemoglobin levels were <110 g/L in 33% of infants fed animal milk, compared to 13% and 11% in those receiving non-iron-fortified and iron-fortified formula, respectively. Iron deficiency was observed in 43% of children consuming animal milk.
